title: AI anthropomorphism
summary:
AI anthropomorphism is the attribution of human-like feelings, mental states, and behavioral characteristics to artificial intelligence systems. Factors related to the user of the AI, such as culture, age, education, gender, and personality traits, are also important determinants of the phenomenon.

Views of artificial agents possessing human-like intelligence have existed since the early development of computers in the mid-1900s. The use of the human mind as a metaphor for understanding the workings of machine systems was prevalent among researchers in the early days of computer science. Among the most widely cited papers of this period was Alan Turing's "Computing Machinery and Intelligence," in which he introduced the Turing Test. The AI boom of the 2020s brought about the widespread emergence of generative AI; chatbots such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude based on large language models have become increasingly pervasive, and research has shown that humans are often unable to distinguish human-generated text from AI-generated text.

In one sample of U.S. adults from 2024, two-thirds of people believed that ChatGPT is possibly conscious on some level. A 2025 study found that women, people of color, and older individuals were most likely to anthropomorphize AI, and that anthropomorphic attributions to AI had increased by 34% in the past year. A YouGov poll reported that 46% of Americans believe people should display politeness to AI chatbots by saying "please" and "thank you." Among the most extreme incidents occurred in 2022, when engineer Blake Lemoine publicly claimed that Google's LaMDA was conscious; his claims were widely dismissed and Google fired him.

The early ELIZA chatbot demonstrated this phenomenon: despite using constrained Rogerian psychotherapist dialogue that simply mirrored user statements, people related to the program in anthropomorphic ways as though it was a person. Academic research has examined negative dimensions of AI anthropomorphism, showing it can exaggerate AI capabilities as a form of hype and distort moral judgments about AI as a fallacy.
